newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crude outlook-heating oil rules upside tests.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crude outlook-heating oil rules upside tests.

text.p: U.S. crudes will rally as high as heating oil allows, according to traders and analysts, who predicted crude's direction this week depended on how much fundamental strength remained in the products.

Sentiment in the market calls for November NYMEX crude prices to forge tests of new post-Gulf War highs at $26 a barrel, a level that if broken and sustained could lead to further price spikes of $1.00 or more, traders said.
Rita Beale, oil analyst for Fimat in Houston, was looking for a close above the $25.70 a barrel mark to release a new round of speculative buying for the November futures contract.
"We are poised, but not certain to go higher," Beale said.
What keeps the market bullish is obvious: extremely low distillate inventories heading into the winter, making heating prices vulnerable to cold weather jolts.
"This is all a product-led rally. I don't see anything from keeping it going higher," said Bill O'Grady, oil analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis.

Short supplies of distillates have included an overlooked factor, which is strong demand for diesel, O'Grady said. Oil usually made into heating oil has been instead turned into diesel fuel for trains, trucks, barges and ships.
O'Grady said heating oil prices traditionally pull back at this time of the year, and "consolidate somewhat."
This year, that has not happened, leaving spot NYMEX heating oil near the 74.00 cents a gallon level, crack spreads well-supported, and crude along for the heating oil ride.
For cash crude, domestic traders said grade differentials looked to be bouyant again for the start of the week, notably for light crudes, where a rally in Louisiana barrels was seen late last week.

Throughput reductions at the British Petroleum refinery in Toledo, Ohio prompted talk of surplus Heavy and Light Louisiana Sweet becoming available, but traders said demand appeared to be offsetting additional barrels.
Otherwise, refiners were content to hold onto the barrels they had.
"The market has been active, but not with huge volumes. Refiners are really not turning things around," said a Texas trader.

Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James and Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire firmed to trade at or near a 70 cents premium to West Texas Intermediate, some 20-25 cents higher for the rallying Heavy Louisiana Sweet compared with the prior week.
